name: Chlorophyll internal deodorant
lead: Chlorophyll internal deodorant refers to the oral use of chlorophyll or its water-soluble semi-synthetic derivatives, chlorophyllins, to reduce body, breath or waste odor. Chlorophyllins are salts made from chlorophyll, and the main food-additive forms are sodium chlorophyllins, listed as E140(ii) and E141(ii).[1]

Oral preparations have been marketed for odor from incontinence, colostomies and body odor generally.[1] The Wikipedia article on the topic flags this claim as lacking medical citation and cites no controlled human trials of body, ostomy or fecal odor.[1] Laboratory and animal research on chlorophyllin has mostly concerned binding of mutagens rather than odor.[1]

paras: In the 1940s the researcher F. Howard Westcott described chlorophyll as an odor blocker. Between about 1950 and 1953 companies added it to toothpaste, sanitary products and soap, mainly in advertising, and brands dropped it quickly afterwards.[1] The Wikipedia article states that the hype was later judged unwarranted and that the underlying research may have been a hoax.[1]
In the 2020s social media influencers revived it as 'chlorophyll water'; Wikipedia describes the medical claims made for it as unsubstantiated.[1]
Body-odor guidance lists chlorophyllin ointments, sprays and supplements among agents that have been used, alongside antiperspirants, deodorants and antibacterial soaps.[2]
No studies found. The Wikipedia entry cites no controlled human trials of chlorophyllin for body, ostomy or fecal odor; related research is in vitro or animal work on other effects.[1]

timeline.event: F. Howard Westcott's research describes chlorophyll as an odor blocker.[1]
Chlorophyll used in toothpaste, sanitary towels and soap marketing.[1]
Revived on social media as 'chlorophyll water'.[1]

card.summary: Oral chlorophyll or chlorophyllin pitched as an internal deodorant; the cited human evidence for body odor is essentially absent.
card.note: No controlled human trials for body odor found in cited sources.

quick.overview:
Chlorophyll and chlorophyllin are green plant-pigment products sold as oral 'internal deodorants' for body, breath and waste odor. The idea dates to the 1940s and returned via social media in the 2020s.

The cited reference material lists no controlled human trials of the odor claim.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say it neutralizes odor-causing compounds from within. Laboratory research has shown chlorophyllin binding some mutagens, but this has not been shown to apply to body odor.
quick.risks: The cited sources contain no safety discussion. It is sold as a supplement and used as a food colorant (E140/E141).
